legend: There are n2%%ZSMJ0%% points on the coordinate plane, at the locations (1,1),(1,2),⋯(1,n),(2,1),(2,2),⋯(2,n),⋮⋮⋱⋮(n,1),(n,2),⋯(n,n).%%ZSMJ1%% More formally, the initial set of points S={(i,j)∣1≤i,j≤n}%%ZSMJ2%%.
You want to move each point to a different point such that
the distance each point moves is at least √d%%ZSMJ3%%, and

the set of resulting points equals the set of initial points. That is, after all the points have moved, they occupy the same locations as before. (More formally, the final set of points equals S%%ZSMJ4%%.)
Given n%%ZSMJ5%% and d%%ZSMJ6%%, find any such movement or report that it does not exist.
input: The first line contains a single integer t%%ZSMJ7%% (1≤t≤150%%ZSMJ8%%) — the number of test cases.

The only line of each test case contains two space-separated integers n%%ZSMJ9%% and d%%ZSMJ10%% (2≤n≤300%%ZSMJ11%%, 1≤d≤109%%ZSMJ12%%) — the range of points and the square of the minimum distance each point must move, respectively.
The sum of n%%ZSMJ13%% over all test cases does not exceed 300%%ZSMJ14%%.
output: For each test case, if such a movement is impossible, output NO.

Otherwise, output YES followed by n2%%ZSMJ15%% lines. Each line should contain four space separated integers xi%%ZSMJ16%%, yi%%ZSMJ17%%, x′i%%ZSMJ18%%, y′i%%ZSMJ19%% (1≤xi,yi,x′i,y′i≤n%%ZSMJ20%%), representing that the point (xi,yi)%%ZSMJ21%% moves to the point (x′i,y′i)%%ZSMJ22%%. The resulting points should satisfy the conditions in the problem statement.
If there are multiple possible movements, print any of them.
